message.content:
**The three “great” schisms that have shaped Christian history**

| # | Schism | Approximate date | Key parties | Main theological / political fault line |
|---|--------|------------------|-------------|----------------------------------------|
| 1 | **The Great Schism (East‑West Schism)** | 1054 CE | Roman Catholic Church (West) vs. Eastern Orthodox Church (East) | Mutual excommunications over papal primacy, the Filioque clause, liturgical practices, and cultural‑political differences. |
| 2 | **The Protestant Reformation** | 1517–1648 CE | Roman Catholic Church vs. emerging Protestant movements (Lutheran, Calvinist, Anglican, Anabaptist, etc.) | Doctrinal disputes over justification, the authority of Scripture vs. tradition, indulgences, and church governance; ultimately a split that produced a wide array of Protestant denominations. |
| 3 | **The Chalcedonian Schism (East‑West Schism of 451 CE)** | 451 CE | Chalcedonian churches (Roman Catholic & Eastern Orthodox) vs. Non‑Chalcedonian (Oriental Orthodox) churches | The Council of Chalcedon’s definition of Christ’s two natures (divine and human) was rejected by several Eastern churches, leading to the formation of the Oriental Orthodox communion (Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopian, etc.). |

These three events are often cited as the most consequential fractures in the Christian tradition, each redefining ecclesiastical authority, doctrine, and the very geography of Christianity.
